meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.text: Вика! Ты вообще меня не слушаешь?
examples.trans: Wait, are you not listening to me at all?

examples.text: Или я для тебя пустое место?
examples.trans: Or am I invisible to you?
Vika, did you want to say something?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: Am I talking to a wall?
What? Excuse me.
Vitya, what is going on here, pal?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'here'.

examples.trans: What are you doing out here?

examples.text: Иди скажи ему, что продюсер уже здесь.
examples.trans: Go tell him that my producer is already here.
I'm here.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to do', forming an aspectual pair with 'сделать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: Something has to be done.
What are you doing out here?
Dima, hi. What are you doing?

meanings.note: Everyday conversational Russian interj meaning 'hi', frequent in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dima, hi. What are you doing?
Hi there. Are you hungry?
Say hello to Dad, we will call.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('yes') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: No, nothing at all.
Oh, just family stuff.
It doesn't seem so.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('nothing') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: No, nothing at all.
Oh, nothing much.
What do you mean, nothing?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'how'.

examples.trans: How are things with you?
As you can see, not bad.
What do you mean, nothing?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'at' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: We have an ideal family.

examples.text: У нас разве не все гости побывали?
examples.trans: Haven't all the important guests visited us already?
Our deadlines are burning.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('I') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: I still work as a cook.
I finally proposed to Vika.

examples.text: Вика! Ты вообще меня не слушаешь?
examples.trans: Wait, are you not listening to me at all?

meanings.note: Abstract masculine noun formed with the productive Slavic suffix '-ость' denoting a quality or state ('guest').

examples.text: Завтра к нам придёт очень важный гость.
examples.trans: Tomorrow a very important guest is coming to us.

examples.text: У нас разве не все гости побывали?
examples.trans: Haven't all the important guests visited us already?
I have that important guest today, remember?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'today'.

examples.trans: I have that important guest today, remember?
Tonight she is definitely going to cook.

examples.text: Дмитрий Владимирович, вы же сегодня на съёмках?
examples.trans: Dmitry Vladimirovich, aren't you at a shoot today?

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (root 'мнить'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to remember'.

examples.trans: I have that important guest today, remember?
Of course I remember.
Do you remember?

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'of course'.

examples.trans: Of course I remember.
Of course I will cook.
I can cook, of course.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('not') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Вика! Ты вообще меня не слушаешь?
examples.trans: Wait, are you not listening to me at all?
It does not matter.

examples.text: Тебе это на канал не пропустят.
examples.trans: They will not let that on television.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to be'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: You need to act more natural, understand?
I will not distract you.

examples.text: Мой карьерный рост был долгим и трудным.
examples.trans: My career climb was long and difficult.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.text: У нас разве не все гости побывали?
examples.trans: Haven't all the important guests visited us already?
No, not all of them wanted this.

examples.text: Меня не будет, я весь день на съёмках.
examples.trans: I won't be here, I'm at a shoot all day.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'day', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: For a couple of days.

examples.text: Нужно пройти обследование через два дня.
examples.trans: We need to take a medical check-up in two days.
Two whole days?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.text: Тебе это на канал не пропустят.
examples.trans: They will not let that on television.
For a couple of days.
Set a reminder on your phone.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'day', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Меня не будет, я весь день на съёмках.
examples.trans: I won't be here, I'm at a shoot all day.

examples.text: Дмитрий Владимирович, вы же сегодня на съёмках?
examples.trans: Dmitry Vladimirovich, aren't you at a shoot today?

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'don't', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Я тебя прошу, Витя, не облажайся.
examples.trans: I am begging you, Vitya, don't mess this up.
I said do not mess it up.
Mind you don't mess up.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (root 'мотреть'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to look', forming an aspectual pair with 'посмотреть'.

examples.trans: Mind you don't mess up.
Look what I've got.
I'm watching TV.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (root 'езжать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to come', forming an aspectual pair with 'приехать'.

examples.trans: Come over in the evening.
Mum arrives tomorrow.
Well, come in the evening.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'with' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: Am I talking to a wall?
With me in the leading role.
I will talk to Nagiyev.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'agreement', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: I will talk to Nagiyev.

examples.text: Я же сказал, договорюсь с Нагиевым.
examples.trans: I told you, I will make a deal with Nagiyev.
I reached an agreement with Nagiyev.

meanings.note: Prefix 'до-' marks reaching a boundary or finishing the remainder of an action (root 'говориться'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to agree', forming an aspectual pair with 'договариваться'.

examples.text: Я же сказал, договорюсь с Нагиевым.
examples.trans: I told you, I will make a deal with Nagiyev.
I reached an agreement with Nagiyev.
We'll arrange something for tomorrow.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to wait', forming an aspectual pair with 'подождать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Виктор Петрович, мы не можем долго ждать.
examples.trans: Viktor Petrovich, we cannot wait that long.
I am waiting for you in the kitchen.
Don't wait for me.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: Keep trying hard, Lena Pavlovna.
I will not distract you.

examples.text: Вы уж извините, что так вышло.
examples.trans: Please forgive me that it turned out this way.

examples.trans: I do not meddle in your kitchen.
